claims.text: In single-phase high-entropy alloys, toughness retention is governed by the degree of local lattice-strain heterogeneity created by chemical short-range order.
Homogenization heat treatment can reduce chemical short-range order and associated lattice-strain heterogeneity.
A minor compositional adjustment can disrupt short-range order and reduce local lattice-strain variation.
Heterogeneous lattice strain modulates dislocation behavior, including cross-slip.
Reducing short-range order decreases localized regions of high lattice strain.
Reducing lattice-strain heterogeneity promotes more spatially uniform dislocation motion and cross-slip.
Nano-twinning can act as an additional deformation mode that helps retain toughness in CrCoNi.
A more uniform distribution of plastic deformation delays crack nucleation and propagation.
Delaying crack nucleation and propagation improves toughness retention under mechanical load.
The homogenized alloy will have a higher fracture toughness, measured by K_IC, than the as-cast or standard-processed baseline.
The homogenized alloy will develop a more uniform distribution of dislocations and nano-twins during deformation than the baseline.
Increasing short-range order and lattice-strain heterogeneity produces concentrated stress fields, earlier crack initiation, and reduced toughness.
As-cast single-phase CrCoNi or Cantor alloys exhibit measurable chemical short-range-order variations and associated lattice-strain heterogeneity.
Local strain variations in the baseline can promote distributed plasticity while also creating stress concentrations that facilitate crack initiation.
The proposed behavior applies to single-phase FCC and BCC solid-solution high-entropy alloys up to about 800 degrees Celsius, provided phase stability is maintained.
The proposed behavior may cease to govern toughness when multiphase transformations or extrinsic mechanisms such as precipitation hardening dominate.
